title: Old age
hook: honoring the old: Confucius waits for the elders with staffs, and the Torah says rise
tomorrow: an old man, nearly blind, crossed his hands to bless. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: stepping back. Kunti walked to the forest gladly, so her sons could step in. Today, the ones who stepped back, and what's owed to them.

At some weddings, the oldest aunt gets the best chair and the first plate, and nobody has to say why. Confucius would have noticed. The Analects keep a small scene from his village. When the villagers were drinking together, he didn't leave whenever he felt like it. He waited. When the old people with their walking staffs went out, then he went out, right after them. The book records no speech about it, only the detail, kept by students who were watching.
screen: `THE BEST CHAIR, THE FIRST PLATE.` → `A VILLAGE FEAST.` → `CONFUCIUS WAITS.` → `THE STAFFS GO OUT FIRST.`

segments.voice: So, today's question: what's owed to the old? Confucius's answer starts with a word, xiao, usually translated filial piety: the reverence children owe their parents. Its partner, ti, is the respect the young owe their elders. He's blunt about what it isn't. A student asks him about it, and he says: these days it means feeding your parents. But dogs and horses get fed too. Without reverence, what's the difference? Another student asks, and he says the hard part is the face: doing the chores isn't enough if you do them with a sour look. So honor, for Confucius, lives in the body and the manner. You wait, you mind your face, you let the old go first, and you mean it. Even leaving a party was a lesson. Here's a neighbor who says something close. The Torah: "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD." Shared: honor you can see. Stand up. Look them in the face. And one honest difference. For Confucius, the root is the family and the rites of the village; reverence for elders grows out of reverence for your own parents. Leviticus ties it straight to God, and to every gray head, kin or stranger. Both put honor where it can be seen.
screen: `XIAO: REVERENCE FOR PARENTS.` · `DOGS AND HORSES GET FED TOO.` · `THE TORAH: RISE UP.` · `FAMILY RITES, OR GOD'S COMMAND.` · then, large: `HONOR THE OLD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one elder you haven't seen in a while: a grandparent, a neighbor, an old teacher. Picture them walking into the room, and sit up a little taller, as if you'd just risen for them. Choose one question you'd ask about their life when you next visit. Then sit quietly with their face in mind for the rest of the time.
Old age: in Confucius's teaching, honor for parents and elders shown in the body, waiting until the elders with staffs have gone out.
Your line: honor the old. Rise before the gray head, and wait for the staffs to go first. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Confucian tradition calls reverence for parents xiao, filial piety, and pairs it with ti, respect for elders, both shown in manner as well as support. The Torah commands rising before the aged (Leviticus 19:32), and some Jews still stand when an elder enters the room.
